items.headline: Iran steps up attacks on Hormuz shipping as the US weighs naval escorts and a third carrier group
items.summary: Reports count about 40 drone and missile attacks a week on commercial ships in the strait, with three tankers hit and one set ablaze. Tanker freight rates are roughly twenty times pre-war levels; the US says it could escort vessels with a coalition.
items.rationale: Attacks keep war-risk insurance and freight costs extreme even as some flows resume. Energy importers in Asia and Europe pay most; producers outside the Gulf earn more per barrel. Escalation risk is two-sided: escorts could ease flows or widen the conflict.

industries.why: Freight and war-risk premiums at extreme levels
Supply risk keeps crude prices elevated
Energy and shipping inputs cost more

economies.why: Large crude importer exposed to Gulf supply
Relies on Gulf crude and LNG
Net energy exporter gains on terms of trade

items.headline: Crude exports through Hormuz near pre-war levels and LNG transits hit a wartime high
items.summary: Gulf crude exports have largely recovered as more tankers transit, and September LNG shipments through the strait were the highest since the war began. Iran's own tanker loadings fell to zero under the US blockade.
items.rationale: Recovering Gulf volumes cap the upside for oil and LNG prices and ease shortages for Asian and European buyers. The recovery is fragile while attacks continue, so prices stay volatile.

industries.why: Gas supply relief for heavy users

items.headline: US sanctions Iran's car, rail and metals sectors and a Russia-linked network that moved $17 billion
items.summary: The Treasury targeted Iran's two largest carmakers, its state railway and metals firms, and designated a Russia-linked shadow banking network that processed more than $17 billion for Iran between January 2025 and June 2026.
items.rationale: Pressure shifts from sea to land, cutting Iran's remaining revenue. Secondary-sanction risk rises for banks and traders in China, Russia and the Gulf that handle Iranian flows, adding compliance costs.

items.headline: EU weighs emergency diesel release as the US taps its final 40 million barrels of crude reserves
items.summary: The US asked Europe for a 120 million-barrel diesel drawdown over six months and warned of a possible diesel export ban. The US is releasing the last 40 million barrels of a 172 million-barrel reserve drawdown, with diesel above $6 a gallon.
items.rationale: Reserve releases ease near-term fuel prices but leave thinner buffers if supply shocks worsen. A US export ban would hit European fuel users hard; diesel costs flow straight into freight and farm costs.

industries.why: Diesel is the main fuel cost

items.headline: Euro-area inflation jumps to 3.8%, a three-year high, as energy prices rise 18.8%
items.summary: September flash inflation beat the 3.6% forecast; energy explained close to half of it, and prices rose 0.6% in the month alone.
items.rationale: Raises the odds of another ECB hike after September's move to 2.5%, tightening credit for households and firms. Lenders gain margin; property and consumer spending take the hit.

industries.why: Higher rate expectations lift mortgage costs

items.headline: US factory input prices jump to 77.9, their highest since the Iran war began, as activity holds at 54.5
items.summary: The ISM prices index rose 6.8 points while the headline manufacturing index slipped to 54.5. Employment kept expanding; the September jobs report is due on 2 October.
items.rationale: Strong activity plus fast-rising input costs keeps another Fed hike in play, supporting yields and the dollar. Margin pressure grows for manufacturers that can't pass costs on.

industries.why: Input costs rising faster than prices

items.headline: US 10-year yield holds near 24-year highs and 30-year near its highest since 2004
items.summary: Stocks edged up at the start of October as yields eased slightly, but long-term borrowing costs remain near multi-decade highs and markets price roughly a two-in-three chance of an October Fed hike.
items.rationale: High long-term yields reprice mortgages, corporate debt and long-duration growth assets, and draw capital toward the dollar, pressuring emerging-market currencies.

industries.why: Mortgage and cap rates reprice higher

items.headline: UK 30-year gilt yield breaks 6% for the first time since 1998 ahead of the 28 October budget
items.summary: Long gilts sold off on energy-driven inflation, expected Bank of England tightening, £252 billion of planned issuance and active central-bank gilt sales of about £46 billion a year.
items.rationale: Rising debt-service costs constrain fiscal room before the budget and push up mortgage and corporate borrowing costs. Sterling assets stay sensitive to any fiscal surprise.

economies.why: Higher debt costs and fiscal squeeze

items.headline: Japan's big manufacturers report the best sentiment since 2018 on AI and chip demand
items.summary: The Tankan index for large manufacturers rose to +24 from +22, a sixth straight gain, though non-manufacturers slipped to +35. The yen trades near 157 per dollar as US yields above 5.2% offset a narrower rate gap.
items.rationale: Strong factory confidence supports capital spending and gives the Bank of Japan room for further hikes. A weak yen lifts exporters' earnings but raises import costs.

items.headline: Memory chip contract prices set to rise 40–50% this quarter as AI demand absorbs supply
items.summary: Leading producers report memory capacity essentially sold out for 2026, and large cloud buyers are accepting increases of up to 50% while receiving only partial orders.
items.rationale: Chipmakers hold pricing power; device, PC and car makers face rising component costs that squeeze margins or lift shelf prices. Asian chip-producing economies benefit.

items.headline: More than 210 strikes on Black Sea shipping since July make it the most dangerous since Russia's invasion
items.summary: A maritime-risk firm counted over 210 attacks on commercial vessels between July and the end of September, disrupting grain exports, as Japan announced further sanctions on Russia.
items.rationale: Black Sea disruption tightens world grain supply and raises shipping insurance, adding to food inflation already pushed up by fertiliser costs.

items.headline: OPEC+ expected to hold November output targets at its 4 October meeting
items.summary: Eight members are expected to roll over targets, though actual production stays below quota because of wartime disruption.
items.rationale: An unchanged target signals no new supply relief, keeping the market reliant on Hormuz flows and reserve releases.

industries.why: No extra supply to cap prices

items.headline: Yuan weakens to 6.71 per dollar on Fed hike bets while China's trade grows 17.6% this year
items.summary: Markets price about a 67% chance of an October Fed hike. China's exports rose 14.6% and imports 22% in the first eight months.
items.rationale: A softer yuan supports exporters, while strong trade growth cushions weak domestic demand and property. Dollar strength still pressures capital flows.

items.headline: India's central bank meets 5–7 October with crude above $100 and the rupee near 96 per dollar
items.summary: The repo rate has stood at 5.25% for four meetings; inflation of about 4.8%, high crude and a weak rupee raise pressure to tighten or defend the currency.
items.rationale: A hike or tighter liquidity would raise borrowing costs for banks, property and consumers; holding risks further rupee weakness and imported inflation.

economies.why: Policy squeeze from oil and the rupee
